subject: chemistry_2
question_text: What are amino acids? Give two examples.

verification.note: Unit 13 (Biomolecules) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", printed chapter 10 "BIOMOLECULES", book pp.99-104; the book prints this question on book p.101 as VSAQ 23. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK WORDING: the printed answer calls amino acids "the building blocks of proteins". That is a figure of speech, so this card says they are the units from which proteins are made. The printed answer also gives no structures; glycine and alanine are written out here.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: An amino acid is an organic compound that
carries both an amino group, –NH₂, and a
In the α-amino acids that make up proteins,
both groups are attached to the same carbon
steps.why: Two groups on the same molecule is the definition, and it is the reason amino acids can join end to end into a protein: the –COOH of one reacts with the –NH₂ of the next. Saying "α-amino acid" fixes where the groups sit, which is what the proteins of the body are made of.
common_mistakes: Naming only one of the two groups. Both –NH₂ and –COOH are needed for the definition.
Leaving out the word α. Amino acids with the groups on different carbon atoms exist but do not build proteins.
steps.memory_tip: Amino for –NH₂, acid for –COOH, both on the same carbon.
steps.margin_note: Write both group formulae, not just their names. That is what the examiner reads for.

steps.label: Examples
lines: Amino acids are the units from which all
proteins are made; about 20 of them occur
in the proteins of the body.
steps.why: Glycine is the simplest amino acid, with a hydrogen atom as its side chain, and alanine is the next simplest, with a methyl group; the pair shows that the side chain is the only part that varies. About 20 of them, in different orders, account for every protein in the body.
common_mistakes: Giving a compound with only one functional group as an example. Acetic acid and methylamine are not amino acids.
Writing that there are 20 amino acids in nature. There are about 20 in proteins; many more exist elsewhere.
steps.memory_tip: Glycine has H as its side chain, alanine has CH₃.
steps.margin_note: Two names finish this mark, but write the structures too: they take one line and prove the definition.

insider_note: Both groups, then two names. Adding the two structures costs one line and turns a memorised answer into a proved one.
